name: Natural Frequencies (Bayesian Reasoning Format)
description: People solve Bayesian problems far more accurately when information is expressed as natural frequencies (for example '10 out of 1,000 people') than as conditional probabilities or percentages.
design_relevance_note: A presentation technique for risk and test-result information: lead with counts out of a stated total rather than percentages; pairs naturally with base-rate disclosure.
myth_risk_note: Well supported as a facilitation effect; the size and the explanation (ecological rationality vs nested-sets) are still debated in the literature the meta-analysis reviews.
prevalence_note: Mainly medical-risk communication and statistical-literacy work.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of 35 articles (226 performance estimates) finds people solve descriptive Bayesian inference tasks better when information is given as natural frequencies than as conditional probabilities; short menu formats and visual aids showed some of the strongest moderation effects, improving performance for both formats.
findings.effect_size: 35 articles, 226 performance estimates (magnitude not given in the abstract)
findings.source_title: Meta-analysis of the effect of natural frequencies on Bayesian reasoning.

findings.description: In two studies, training people to construct frequency representations of Bayesian problems produced a higher immediate learning effect and greater long-term stability than teaching Bayes's rule, though rule training was as good for transfer to new problems.
findings.source_title: Teaching Bayesian reasoning in less than two hours.
